awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Cutting-Edge Nitride Based Distributed Bragg IR-Reflectors
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial impacts of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project lie in advancing laser targeting, range finding, light detection and ranging (LIDAR), free-space optical communication, and active sensing. The development of nitride-based reflectors will provide enhanced durability, efficiency, and optical performance. The global high-power laser market is expanding rapidly, with increasing demand for reliable, long-lasting optical components. This project will contribute to scientific and economic progress by advancing technological knowledge in semiconductor materials, optoelectronics, and photonics. This technology has wide-ranging applications that include improving national security by enhancing military laser systems, increasing the precision of LIDAR-based remote sensing for autonomous vehicles and improving industrial systems. Beyond these technical advancements, this project is expected to generate high-tech jobs in semiconductor manufacturing, laser system design, and research and development. The commercialization of this technology will foster economic growth and reduce energy consumption in laser-based systems. By integrating these advanced reflectors into various industries, this project will support long-term technological progress, strengthening the broader scientific community, and contributing to innovation-driven economic development.

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project focuses on developing highly reflective nitride-based Distributed Bragg Reflectors (DBRs) for infrared applications. Current oxide-based reflectors suffer from limited efficiency, laser damage susceptibility, and broad reflection bands, which hinder performance in high-power laser applications. To overcome these challenges, this project will utilize nitride single crystals with varying compositions to achieve more than 99.5% narrow band reflectivity at 1030-1070 nm enabling high-power laser resistance. By fine-tuning layer thickness and composition, we aim to achieve superior optical performance while minimizing point and extended defects formation. Advanced metal-organic chemical vapor deposition techniques will be employed, optimizing growth parameters such as temperature and metal organic flow rates along with the use of nitride native substrates to control film quality. Substrate removal and wafer bonding techniques will be explored to integrate nitride DBRs with silicon and other materials, ensuring compatibility and stability. The project will develop high-performance, crack-free nitride reflectors consisting of AlInN/GaN multilayers, achieving 99.5% reflection and a 40 nm stopband at ~1050 nm. These advancements will enable practical deployment in high-intensity IR environments, supporting next-generation laser technologies.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
High-performance laser systems used in optical communications, precision sensing, ranging, and emerging defense technologies depend on mirrors capable of reflecting nearly all incident light while maintaining stability under demanding operating conditions. Semiconductor-based distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) offer a promising alternative to conventional optical mirrors, particularly for high-power applications requiring exceptional thermal stability, durability, and optical performance. However, manufacturing these structures remains challenging because achieving extremely high reflectivity requires precise control of composition, thickness, and crystalline quality across many alternating semiconductor layers.

This NSF STTR Phase I project, led by NovaTech Innovations in collaboration with the University of South Florida and supported by the advanced fabrication and characterization capabilities of the Stanford Nanofabrication Facility, made significant progress toward developing next-generation nitride semiconductor mirrors for near-infrared wavelengths around 1050 nm.

Throughout Phase I, the research team conducted an extensive experimental program involving epitaxial growth, structural characterization, optical measurements, and iterative process optimization. Advanced techniques, including scanning electron microscopy, high-resolution X-ray diffraction, atomic force microscopy, secondary ion mass spectrometry, and spectroscopic ellipsometry, were used to investigate material quality, layer uniformity, and optical behavior. These investigations identified critical limitations in the initial mirror architecture and enabled the development of a revised, non-quarter-wave design that substantially improved structural quality and scalability.

A major Phase I achievement was the successful growth of a 24-pair AlInN/GaN semiconductor mirror exhibiting planar interfaces without the V-shaped defects observed in earlier structures at the two cross-sectional locations examined. This result represents an important technical advancement over earlier project runs and directly addresses one of the principal barriers to manufacturing high-reflectivity nitride mirrors: maintaining crystalline integrity and interface uniformity as the number of layers increases.

Importantly, Phase I transformed the project's central technical challenge into a defined and actionable development pathway for Phase II. Rather than simply increasing the number of layers in an architecture prone to defects, the team established a revised design and growth process capable of producing a substantially thicker, structurally improved multilayer stack. Supporting optical calculations indicate that very high reflectivity is achievable by extending the optimized architecture to additional layer pairs. These findings provide a compelling basis for Phase II investigations focused on increasing the pair count, aligning the optical stopband with the target wavelength, experimentally validating high reflectivity, evaluating high-power performance, and advancing integration with silicon substrates.

Beyond its technical accomplishments, the project strengthened domestic expertise in advanced semiconductor photonics and established a productive collaboration among a technology-focused small business, an academic research institution, and a nationally recognized nanofabrication facility. The program provided valuable hands-on training in semiconductor epitaxy, process engineering, advanced materials characterization, and optical analysis, while developing practical capabilities that can support future research, commercialization, and workforce development.

Overall, Phase I successfully reduced key technical uncertainties, demonstrated a promising route to improved multilayer crystal quality, and established the scientific and engineering foundation needed for Phase II advancement. The next phase offers an opportunity to build on these experimentally validated achievements, demonstrate the targeted optical performance, and advance the technology toward scalable manufacturing and applications in high-power lasers, precision photonics, sensing, and national security. Successful Phase II development could contribute to an important domestic capability in high-performance semiconductor optical components.
